screens.title: Centralized Logging with CloudWatch Logs and Kinesis Firehose
screens.narratorSegment: Logging is the foundation of observability. In this lesson you'll learn how CloudWatch Logs centralizes events from AWS services and your custom systems, how Logs Insights helps you query and troubleshoot interactively, and how subscription filters plus Kinesis Firehose enable real-time processing and durable delivery to analytics stores. We'll show concrete examples: installing the CloudWatch Agent on EC2 to send application files, writing Logs Insights queries to find errors and aggregate counts, configuring a subscription filter to stream only relevant events to a Lambda function, and using Firehose to deliver compressed, time-partitioned files to S3 for Athena queries. You'll also see common mistakes, such as missing IAM permissions or improper filter patterns, and practical remedies. By the end you will understand both the operational steps and the design choices that balance cost, latency, and durability — and you will be able to design a pipeline that supports alerting, enrichment, and archival without losing observability. Consider a simple question as we begin: which logs are critical to retain, and for how long?

screens.title: CloudWatch Logs: Groups, Streams, and Retention
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch Logs centralizes events from AWS services and custom hosts. A log group is a logical container with shared retention, tags, and access control. Inside a log group, a log stream is an ordered sequence of log events that typically maps to a single source, for example an EC2 instance, a container task, or a Lambda invocation. Choosing a sensible naming convention for log groups and streams matters because it makes discovery easier and simplifies applying retention policies. Retention controls how long CloudWatch stores logs: shorter retention reduces cost but may violate compliance or make post-incident forensics harder. A common approach is to set shorter retention for verbose debug logs and longer retention for security or audit logs. Example: keep access logs for one year for analytics, but keep transient debug logs for seven days. A common misconception is thinking streams are automatically permanent; streams are ephemeral sequences within a group and the group-level retention applies. Key takeaway: design log groups by function and retention by risk, then verify with a simple lifecycle test. How long would you retain audit logs in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Log group strategy
keyIdea.text: Group logs by application or role, map streams to sources, and set retention policies aligned to compliance and cost goals.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Log Groups & Retention
Definition & Best Practices
A log group groups related streams. Streams are sequences from a single source. Apply retention at the group level to manage cost and compliance.
Naming convention
Use /service/environment/component, for example /myapp/prod/nginx-access
Retention policy
Set shorter retention for debug logs, longer for audit logs; verify with lifecycle tests.
Common mistake
Forgetting to assign the agent to the correct log group or setting retention too short for critical logs.
Key Takeaway

Design groups by function, map streams to distinct sources, and set retention according to legal and operational needs.

Concrete example
/myapp/prod/access-logs — retention 365 days /myapp/prod/debug-logs — retention 7 days /security/audit — retention Never Expire
Why it matters: time partitioning and naming let you find relevant streams quickly and apply the correct lifecycle to each set of logs.
Check your understanding
If you need to retain security logs for audits, which retention option prevents deletion? (Answer: Never Expire.)

screens.title: Installing and Configuring the CloudWatch Agent
screens.narratorSegment: The CloudWatch Agent reads files and pushes events into CloudWatch Logs. On EC2, install the agent package and provide a JSON configuration that lists the files to collect and the destination log groups and streams. Important fields include file_path, log_group_name, and log_stream_name; you can use {instance_id} to ensure unique streams per host. Also set the agent's metrics collection interval and run-as user. A concrete example: colocate your application logs in /opt/myapp/logs/app. log and configure the agent to send them to /myapp/ec2-logs with log_stream_name set to the instance id. After placing the config file, start the agent and verify logs arrive in the CloudWatch console. Common mistakes are incorrect file paths, forgetting timezone or timestamp_format when logs have custom timestamps, and failing to restart the agent after config changes. Verification: append a test line to the log file and confirm it appears in the configured log stream within a minute. Installing and Configuring the CloudWatch Agent means install the agent, configure collect_list entries with file paths and log group names, use instance placeholders for streams, and verify ingestion.. In practical terms, collect files from ec2 and containers using a json agent config. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Agent essentials
keyIdea.text: Install the agent, configure collect_list entries with file paths and log group names, use instance placeholders for streams, and verify ingestion.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › CloudWatch Agent
Example agent config
Save as /etc/amazon/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/config.json and then start the agent.
{
  "agent": {
    "metrics_collection_interval": 60,
    "run_as_user": "root"
  },
  "logs": {
    "logs_collected": {
      "files": {
        "collect_list": [
          {
            "file_path": "/var/log/messages",
            "log_group_name": "/ec2/messages",
            "log_stream_name": "{instance_id}",
            "timezone": "UTC"
          },
          {
            "file_path": "/opt/myapp/logs/access.log",
            "log_group_name": "/myapp/access-logs",
            "log_stream_name": "{instance_id}",
            "timezone": "UTC",
            "timestamp_format": "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"
          }
        ]
      }
    },
    "log_stream_name": "{instance_id}"
  }
}
After saving the config, run the agent control command to apply it and check CloudWatch for events.
Commands and verification
sudo yum install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent # create a sample log and restart agent sudo mkdir -p /opt/myapp/logs sudo echo "INFO: Application started" | sudo tee -a /opt/myapp/logs/app.log sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -a append-config -m ec2 -c file:/tmp/config.json -s
Common mistakes
Wrong file path, missing timestamp format for custom timestamps, and not restarting the agent after editing the config.

screens.title: CloudWatch Logs Insights: Querying and Parsing
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch Logs Insights provides an interactive query language for analyzing log data. Begin with a broad filter and progressively narrow it. The basic building blocks are filter to limit events, parse to extract fields from message text, stats to aggregate, and sort/limit to manage results. For example, you can filter for ERROR messages using a regular expression, parse out a request id to group by user activity, and then use stats count by time bin to see frequency. A step-by-step pattern: 1) select the target log group, 2) filter for the symptom text, 3) parse required fields using a simple pattern, 4) run stats to aggregate. A common misconception is to run highly specific queries first; start broad to ensure you capture variations. Example query from the source finds error messages, extracts request_id, and counts occurrences per minute. Use limit to keep results fast and avoid overwhelming the console. Key takeaway: Logs Insights helps you iterate quickly and find root causes without exporting logs. CloudWatch Logs Insights: Querying and Parsing means start broad with filter, extract fields with parse, aggregate with stats, and always use limit to keep queries responsive.. In practical terms, use filter, parse, and stats to find and summarize events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Start broad with filter, extract fields with parse, aggregate with stats, and always use limit to keep queries responsive.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Logs Insights
Query example
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @logStream like /ERROR/
| parse @message "Request ID: *" as request_id
| stats count(*) by request_id, bin(1m)
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 20
Explanation: filter finds candidate events, parse extracts a field, stats groups and counts by time bin, and limit prevents large result sets.
Tips and pitfalls
  • Start broad; refine with filters to avoid missing variant messages.
  • Use parse with simple patterns; complex regex can be slow.
  • Always apply limit and binning to keep queries responsive.
Example scenario
Find all errors in the last five minutes and count by request id to find a failing client or API endpoint.

screens.title: Subscription Filters: Real-time Routing of Log Events
screens.narratorSegment: Subscription filters create a live stream of selected log events from a log group to a destination such as Lambda, Kinesis Data Streams, or Kinesis Firehose. The central parameter is the filterPattern. An empty pattern sends all events; a specific pattern like ERROR or [event_type=ERROR] restricts forwarding and reduces downstream costs. Use subscription filters when you need real-time alerting, enrichment, or forwarding to SIEMs. Typical use cases include forwarding security logs to a threat detection pipeline, sending only error-level events to a Lambda that triggers notifications, or streaming everything to Firehose for archival. When attaching a subscription to a Log Group, ensure the destination has the correct permissions and the role ARN is configured. A common misconception is that subscription filters store events; they do not—they stream events as they arrive. Also be aware that if you forward high-volume events without filtering, downstream systems may be overloaded or incur large costs. Key takeaway: design filter patterns to balance necessary visibility with downstream capacity and cost. Subscription Filters: Real-time Routing of Log Events means use filter patterns to control which events are forwarded in real time; empty patterns forward everything and specific patterns reduce cost and load.. In practical terms, filter patterns and destinations for streaming events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Subscription Filters
How subscription filters work
Define a filter pattern on a log group and send matching events to a destination in real time.
Destination
Lambda, Kinesis, or Firehose
Filter Pattern
Empty (all) or specific patterns like "ERROR" or structured patterns for fields.
Permissions
Destination must allow CloudWatch Logs to deliver using the provided role ARN.
Example AWS CLI
aws logs put-subscription-filter \\
  --log-group-name MyLogGroup \\
  --filter-name MyLambdaSubscriptionFilter \\
  --filter-pattern "" \\
  --destination-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:MyLogProcessorFunction \\
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/CloudWatchLogsLambdaAccessRole
Quick rules
  • Empty filter forwards everything.
  • Specific patterns lower cost and load.
  • Verify role permissions to avoid delivery failures.
Check your understanding
When would you use an empty pattern? When you need to deliver all events, for example to an archival Firehose pipeline.

screens.title: Using Lambda to Process Subscription Events
screens.narratorSegment: When CloudWatch Logs forwards events to Lambda, the payload is base64 encoded and gzipped. Your Lambda code must decode and decompress the payload, then parse the JSON structure to access logEvents. A simple Python example decodes base64, decompresses gzip, and loads JSON; then you can inspect message fields, detect patterns, and trigger alerts or enrich data before forwarding. Use this pattern for real-time alerting—detect Access Denied or suspicious patterns and notify an on-call system. A frequent misconception is expecting plain text; if you print the raw event you will see encoded data. Also ensure your Lambda has the logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents permissions so it can produce its own logs. Example code from the chapter demonstrates decoding and printing events; in practice you would replace prints with enrichment or forwarding code. Takeaway: Lambda gives flexible per-event actions but be mindful of execution time and downstream error handling. Using Lambda to Process Subscription Events means subscription payloads are encoded and compressed; decode, decompress, and parse json to access log events for processing.. In practical terms, decode base64 gzipped payloads and extract messages for custom actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lambda decoding
keyIdea.text: Subscription payloads are encoded and compressed; decode, decompress, and parse JSON to access log events for processing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Lambda Processing
Python Lambda Example
import json
import base64
import gzip

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    # Decode and decompress the log data
    compressed_payload = base64.b64decode(event['awslogs']['data'])
    uncompressed_payload = gzip.decompress(compressed_payload)
    payload = json.loads(uncompressed_payload)

    print("Decoded Payload:", json.dumps(payload, indent=2))

    # Process each log event
    for log_event in payload['logEvents']:
        print(f"Log Event Message: {log_event['message']}")

    return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps('Logs processed successfully!')}
Replace prints with enrichment, alerts, or forwarding logic. Watch for Lambda timeouts on high-volume streams.
Practical notes
  • Ensure the Lambda role grants logs:PutLogEvents so the function can write its own logs.
  • Handle partial failures and implement retries or dead-letter queues for lossless processing.
  • Filter at the log group when possible to limit Lambda invocation volume.
Check your understanding
Why must you decode and decompress the subscription payload? Because CloudWatch Logs forwards it base64 encoded and gzipped to save bandwidth and standardize delivery format.

screens.title: Kinesis Firehose Delivery: Buffering, Transformation, and Destinations
screens.narratorSegment: Kinesis Firehose is built for continuous delivery: it buffers incoming records, optionally transforms them with Lambda, compresses them, and writes them to destinations like S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch. Buffer size and buffer interval determine delivery frequency and cost: smaller buffers deliver more frequently with higher per-request cost, larger buffers reduce A P I calls but increase delivery latency. When delivering to S3, Firehose writes time-partitioned folders that make Athena queries straightforward. Important operational steps include attaching an IAM role that grants write permissions to the destination and configuring transformation Lambda if you need to enrich or reformat records. A common mistake is missing S3 write permissions for the Firehose role which causes delivery failures. Another pitfall is setting buffer intervals so large that searching recent logs in S3 becomes inconvenient. Example: use a buffer size of 5 MB and buffer interval of 300 seconds for moderate throughput, and test to find the balance for your workload. screens.title: Designing a Centralized Logging Pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a centralized logging pipeline begins with mapping sources to log groups: decide whether you group by service, environment, or function. For many teams, a service/environment pattern such as /myapp/prod/nginx is clear and stable. Next, decide which streams will be forwarded in real time and which can be archived. Use subscription filters selectively: stream ERROR or SECURITY events to Lambda for immediate alerting while sending full traffic to Firehose for archival. In the next layer, Firehose delivers to S3 with partitioned paths so Athena can perform analysis. Ensure that each step has appropriate IAM roles and that the Firehose role has permission to write to S3 or to load into Redshift. Plan retention and lifecycle transitions in S3 or CloudWatch to control costs. A common misconception is assuming a single pattern fits all sources; instead, tier your pipeline: high-priority events get real-time paths, low-priority logs go to long-term archival. The final design balances latency, cost, and searchability. Reflect: which events in your system need real-time processing versus archival only? screens.title: Real-time Use Cases vs. Archival Workflows
screens.narratorSegment: Centralized logging supports both immediate operational needs and long-term analytics, but these use cases require different designs. Real-time use cases demand low latency and selective forwarding: subscription filters route critical events like errors or security alerts to Lambda for enrichment and notification. The focus is speed and precision; unnecessary volume increases costs and risks throttling. Archival workflows prioritize durability and cost-effectiveness: Firehose collects a continuous stream, buffers and compresses records, then writes time-partitioned files to S3 so analysts can run Athena queries or ingest into Redshift. A common misconception is treating the two as mutually exclusive; often you run both in parallel—filter only what you need for immediate action while archiving everything. Example: stream only "ERROR"/"CRITICAL" to Lambda for PagerDuty, while Firehose receives all messages for later forensic analysis. When designing the pipeline, balance buffer settings, IAM permissions, and retention so real-time paths remain responsive and archives remain queryable. Which events in your system must trigger immediate action? screens.title: Hands-on: From Agent to Firehose and Logs Insights
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks through launching an EC2 instance, installing the CloudWatch Agent, creating a Lambda for decoding subscription payloads, configuring a subscription filter, and running Logs Insights queries. Start by installing the agent and creating a config file that points to /myapp/ec2-logs. Create a small test log file and append messages including ERROR to validate ingestion. Verify by adding more log lines, checking the Lambda logs, and running the Logs Insights query that filters ERROR and counts events per minute. content.html:

Terminal sequence (summary)
# Install agent
sudo yum install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent
# Create sample log
sudo mkdir -p /opt/myapp/logs
sudo echo "ERROR: Database connection failed" | sudo tee -a /opt/myapp/logs/app.log
# Apply agent config and start

  • Log lines appear in the configured log stream.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting centralized logging typically involves three categories: collection errors, subscription/delivery issues, and permission failures. For collection, check that the CloudWatch Agent is installed and running, verify file paths in the config, and ensure timestamp_format is set for nonstandard timestamps. A frequent mistake is forgetting to restart the agent after updating the config. For subscription and delivery: validate your filter pattern—if it’s too narrow you may forward nothing; if it’s empty you may overwhelm downstream systems. Check CloudWatch Logs metrics and subscription metrics to see if events are being sent. For delivery to Firehose, look at the delivery stream monitoring and the destination S3 bucket for signs of failed writes. Permission errors are a common root cause: confirm the role ARN used for subscriptions or for Firehose has the needed write permissions to the destination. Finally, log a small test event and follow it through the pipeline to find where it stops. The testing habit of injecting a traceable event is often the fastest way to find the broken link. screens.title: Operational Tuning: Buffering, Compression, and Cost Controls
screens.narratorSegment: Operational tuning helps you achieve the right trade-offs between latency, cost, and usability. Buffer size and buffer interval in Firehose control how often records are delivered: smaller buffers and shorter intervals lower latency but increase PUT frequency. Compression reduces storage cost in S3 but adds C P U for compression and decompression during queries. Choose a compression format compatible with your analytics tool—e. g., gzip for Athena. Retention policies in CloudWatch reduce storage costs; for S3 archives consider lifecycle transitions to cheaper tiers. Be careful with time-partitioning: partition by year/month/day/hour to make Athena queries efficient, but avoid overly fine partitions that create many small files. For logs that require fast access, keep shorter buffer intervals or route them to OpenSearch for near real-time search. A common misconception is assuming maximum compression always saves money; small files with heavy compression can increase request costs. Test different buffer settings with representative load to find the right balance. Buffer & compression choices
Example defaults: Buffer size 5 MB and Buffer interval 300 seconds. For low-latency needs reduce interval; for cost savings increase buffer size.
Compression
Use gzip for Athena-compatible compressed files. Beware of many small compressed files—combine when possible.
Partitioning
Time-partitioned S3 paths (year/month/day/hour) make queries efficient while keeping objects manageable.

fullNarratorScript:
Logging is the foundation of observability. In this lesson you'll learn how CloudWatch Logs centralizes events from AWS services and your custom systems, how Logs Insights helps you query and troubleshoot interactively, and how subscription filters plus Kinesis Firehose enable real-time processing and durable delivery to analytics stores. We'll show concrete examples: installing the CloudWatch Agent on EC2 to send application files, writing Logs Insights queries to find errors and aggregate counts, configuring a subscription filter to stream only relevant events to a Lambda function, and using Firehose to deliver compressed, time-partitioned files to S3 for Athena queries. You'll also see common mistakes, such as missing IAM permissions or improper filter patterns, and practical remedies. By the end you will understand both the operational steps and the design choices that balance cost, latency, and durability — and you will be able to design a pipeline that supports alerting, enrichment, and archival without losing observability. Consider a simple question as we begin: which logs are critical to retain, and for how long?

By the end of this chapter you will configure agents and subscription filters, use Logs Insights to query events, build a streaming pipeline for real-time processing, and design a Firehose delivery for durable storage. First, you will learn how the CloudWatch Agent monitors files and routes them into log groups and streams so that diverse sources such as EC2, containers, and on-premises servers can feed a single observability plane. Second, you will learn how to author effective Logs Insights queries to extract fields and aggregate counts for troubleshooting. Third, you will implement subscription filters to stream selected events in real time to Lambda or Firehose for alerting and enrichment. Fourth, you will design a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream, adjusting buffer size and IAM roles to deliver compressed, partitioned files to S3 or to forward to Redshift or OpenSearch. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your setup and make targeted improvements. Think about which of these skills will save time during your next incident response.

These objectives continue by focusing on operational practices and verification. You will set log retention policies per log group to control storage cost and meet compliance requirements, and you will design naming conventions so log groups and streams are discoverable. You will practice writing subscription filter patterns so only the necessary events are forwarded, reducing downstream cost and processing load. Finally, you will verify Firehose delivery by checking buffer size and interval settings and confirming the IAM role has write permissions to the destination. For each objective we include a milestone you can use to prove competency: confirm logs appear in the target log group for the agent objective; run a Logs Insights query that returns expected fields for the query objective; trigger a Lambda via subscription filter and inspect the Lambda logs for the subscription objective; and verify S3 objects arrive with the expected time-partitioned path for Firehose. These verification steps turn theory into repeatable practice.

CloudWatch Logs centralizes events from AWS services and custom hosts. A log group is a logical container with shared retention, tags, and access control. Inside a log group, a log stream is an ordered sequence of log events that typically maps to a single source, for example an EC2 instance, a container task, or a Lambda invocation. Choosing a sensible naming convention for log groups and streams matters because it makes discovery easier and simplifies applying retention policies. Retention controls how long CloudWatch stores logs: shorter retention reduces cost but may violate compliance or make post-incident forensics harder. A common approach is to set shorter retention for verbose debug logs and longer retention for security or audit logs. Example: keep access logs for one year for analytics, but keep transient debug logs for seven days. Subscription filters create a live stream of selected log events from a log group to a destination such as Lambda, Kinesis Data Streams, or Kinesis Firehose. Centralized logging supports both immediate operational needs and long-term analytics, but these use cases require different designs. Real-time use cases demand low latency and selective forwarding: subscription filters route critical events like errors or security alerts to Lambda for enrichment and notification. The focus is speed and precision; unnecessary volume increases costs and risks throttling. Archival workflows prioritize durability and cost-effectiveness: Firehose collects a continuous stream, buffers and compresses records, then writes time-partitioned files to S3 so analysts can run Athena queries or ingest into Redshift. A common misconception is treating the two as mutually exclusive; often you run both in parallel—filter only what you need for immediate action while archiving everything. Operational tuning helps you achieve the right trade-offs between latency, cost, and usability. Buffer size and buffer interval in Firehose control how often records are delivered: smaller buffers and shorter intervals lower latency but increase PUT frequency. Compression reduces storage cost in S3 but adds C P U for compression and decompression during queries. Choose a compression format compatible with your analytics tool—e. g., gzip for Athena. Retention policies in CloudWatch reduce storage costs; for S3 archives consider lifecycle transitions to cheaper tiers. Be careful with time-partitioning: partition by year/month/day/hour to make Athena queries efficient, but avoid overly fine partitions that create many small files. For logs that require fast access, keep shorter buffer intervals or route them to OpenSearch for near real-time search. A common misconception is assuming maximum compression always saves money; small files with heavy compression can increase request costs. Test different buffer settings with representative load to find the right balance. Let's summarize the core concepts you should retain. First, CloudWatch Logs centralizes events into log groups and log streams, and you must design naming and retention policies to balance cost and compliance. Second, Logs Insights offers a query language with filter, parse, and stats to troubleshoot and aggregate logs quickly. Third, subscription filters stream matching events to Lambda, Kinesis Data Streams, or Kinesis Firehose for real-time processing or delivery. Fourth, Kinesis Firehose buffers, optionally transforms, compresses, and delivers logs to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch Service; tune buffer size and interval and verify IAM permissions. Finally, use a tiered pipeline: real-time forwarding for alerts and Firehose archival for analytics. These ideas together form a reliable, scalable logging architecture for production environments.
